This page goes with **Chapter 12, Form in Popular Music** of Robert Hutchinson's open textbook
[*Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom*](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/FormInPopularMusic.html). Read each section there
first. The book draws on John Covach's essay "Form in Rock Music" and analyses real songs with timings. Here, the site's backing band
plays each form on made-up chord progressions, so you can hear how it is built without a melody or lyrics.

**How the demos work:** press **▶ Play**. The strip at the bottom of the page shows the bar and the **section** the band is in
("Bar 9 · A2"). Each demo shows its chord grid with the sections labelled, the whole form at once (or one section at a time:
pick it above the grid). The bar being played lights up. The buttons change the form; the band starts the new one from bar 1. As soon as
the band starts, what it will play the whole way through is written out under the grid, section by section, so you can read ahead. Most forms here are **32 bars**, about a minute at this tempo. Listen through at least once.

## 12.1 Verse–chorus form

The most common form in popular music today. The **chorus** has the hook, the part everyone remembers. The **verses** have different
words each time and usually a less memorable tune. Songs often add an introduction, a **pre-chorus** (leading into the chorus), a
**post-chorus**, and a **bridge** (something new, usually once, late in the song). The book also notes that people disagree about what
to call some sections, and that is normal.
[Read 12.1](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/VerseChorusForm.html)

The book separates **simple** verse–chorus form (the verse and chorus use the same chord progression, so only the melody and words
tell them apart) from **contrasting** verse–chorus form (the chorus has its own progression). Here are both, as verse, chorus, verse,
chorus:

<div class="ar-demo" data-view="grid" data-style="rock" data-tempo="116" data-comp="piano" data-on="bass comp drums" data-staves="comp bass" data-choice-label="Form:" data-choices='[{"label":"Contrasting verse–chorus","chart":"Am|F|C|G|Am|F|C|G|F|G|C|Am|F|G|C|C|Am|F|C|G|Am|F|C|G|F|G|C|Am|F|G|C|C","sections":[[1,"Verse"],[9,"Chorus"],[17,"Verse"],[25,"Chorus"]],"opts":{}},{"label":"Simple verse–chorus","chart":"C|G|Am|F|C|G|Am|F|C|G|Am|F|C|G|Am|F|C|G|Am|F|C|G|Am|F|C|G|Am|F|C|G|Am|F","sections":[[1,"Verse"],[9,"Chorus"],[17,"Verse"],[25,"Chorus"]],"opts":{}}]'></div>

In the simple form, nothing in the chords tells you where the chorus starts. The singer's melody and the words would do that, and a
band usually plays the chorus fuller and louder. In the contrasting form you can hear the change of progression at bar 9.

## 12.2 AABA form

The form of Broadway and the Great American Songbook from the 1930s to the 1950s, and of many 1960s songs (the book names
"Yesterday" and "Hey Jude"). There are four sections of **eight bars**. The **A** section is the main tune and comes three times. **B**,
the **bridge** or "middle eight", is the contrast. The whole 32 bars is sometimes called the **refrain** or **chorus**, and some
songs put a **verse** in front of it.
[Read 12.2](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/AABAForm.html)

<div class="ar-demo" data-view="grid" data-style="swing" data-tempo="150" data-comp="piano" data-on="bass comp drums" data-staves="comp bass" data-choices='[{"label":"AABA, 32 bars","chart":"C|Am|Dm|G7|C|Am|Dm G7|C|C|Am|Dm|G7|C|Am|Dm G7|C|E7|E7|Am|Am|D7|D7|Dm|G7|C|Am|Dm|G7|C|Am|Dm G7|C","sections":[[1,"A1"],[9,"A2"],[17,"B (bridge)"],[25,"A3"]],"opts":{}}]'></div>

Notice where the bridge goes: it leaves C, moves through other keys (E7 to Am, D7 to G), and ends on **G7**, the V chord. That makes the
return of A sound like coming home.

## 12.3 ABAC form

Also 32 bars of four eight-bar sections, but the A section comes back only once, halfway through. The book's examples are "White
Christmas", "Someday My Prince Will Come", "When I Fall in Love" and "Star Dust". It also notes ABAB′, where the last section starts like
B and ends differently.
[Read 12.3](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/ABACForm.html)

<div class="ar-demo" data-view="grid" data-style="swing" data-tempo="150" data-comp="piano" data-on="bass comp drums" data-staves="comp bass" data-choices='[{"label":"ABAC, 32 bars","chart":"C|A7|Dm|G7|C|A7|D7|G7|E7|E7|Am|Am|D7|D7|Dm|G7|C|A7|Dm|G7|C|A7|D7|G7|F|Fm|C|A7|Dm|G7|C|C","sections":[[1,"A"],[9,"B"],[17,"A"],[25,"C"]],"opts":{}}]'></div>

The first A ends on G7, so it is open and leads on. Only C, the last section, really ends.

## 12.4 The 12-bar blues

Twelve bars in three lines of four: **I I I I | IV IV I I | V IV I I**. It started in the blues in the early 1900s and was carried
into swing ("In the Mood") and early rock and roll ("Johnny B. Goode", "Hound Dog", "Rock Around the Clock"). The book's table is
"Johnny B. Goode".
[Read 12.4](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/TwelveBarBlues.html) ·
The site's [blues lessons](../lessons/blues-changes.qmd) go further: the quick change, turnarounds and the jazz blues.

## 12.5 Harmonically closed and open sections

A section is **closed** when it ends on the tonic chord (I) and **open** when it ends somewhere else, usually V and sometimes IV. Open
sections lead on to the next section; closed sections can end the song.
[Read 12.5](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/HarmonicallyClosedAndOpenSections.html)

Typical places, from the book:

| Form | Usually closed | Usually open |
|---|---|---|
| AABA | A sections | B (the bridge), ending on V |
| Verse–chorus | the chorus (sometimes) | verse, pre-chorus, bridge |

The same eight bars, closed and then open. Only the last two bars change:

<div class="ar-demo" data-view="grid" data-style="rock" data-tempo="112" data-comp="piano" data-on="bass comp drums" data-staves="comp bass" data-choice-label="Ending:" data-choices='[{"label":"Closed (ends on I)","chart":"C|Am|F|G|C|Am|G|C","opts":{}},{"label":"Open (ends on V)","chart":"C|Am|F|G|C|Am|Dm|G","opts":{}}]'></div>

## Quizzes {#quiz}

**Open or closed?** The band plays one eight-bar section, in different keys, again and again. Does it end on I or not?

<div class="ar-quiz" data-style="rock" data-tempo="112" data-comp="piano" data-on="bass comp drums" data-staves="comp bass" data-choices='[{"label":"Closed (ends on I)","why":"The last bar is the tonic chord: the section could end the song.","charts":["C|F|G|C|Am|F|G7|C","G|Em|C|D|G|C|D7|G","F|Bb|C|F|Dm|Gm|C7|F","D|Bm|G|A|D|G|A7|D","A|D|E|A|F#m|D|E7|A"],"opts":{}},{"label":"Open (ends off I)","why":"The section stops on V (or IV): it wants to go on.","charts":["C|F|C|Am|F|C|Dm|G","G|C|G|Em|C|G|Am|D","F|Dm|Bb|F|Gm|F|Bb|C","D|G|D|Bm|G|D|Em|A","C|Am|F|G|C|Am|G|F"],"opts":{}}]'></div>

**Which form?** The band plays a whole form, chords only. Listen for what comes back and when, then choose. The section names appear in
the strip at the bottom once you have answered.

## 12.6 Practice: real songs

The book's exercise asks for a timeline of two songs: when each section starts, what it is, and how many bars it lasts. Its answers
are in [12.6](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/PopFormPracticeExercises.html). Do the same with any song you know well:

1. Start a timer with the song. Write the time each time something new starts.
2. Count bars: count the beats in fours, and add a mark for every 1.
3. Name each section. Which one has the hook? Which one comes back with the same words? Which comes once?
4. Mark each section open or closed. Does it end on the home chord?

The site's [Timestamp Notes](../tools/timestamp-notes.qmd) tool keeps timed notes against a recording, if you want to save your timeline.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## For teachers

- **The band:** every demo and quiz runs on the site's [Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.qmd) band. The progressions are made up
  for this page, not taken from songs. AABA and ABAC share their bridge so that the only difference is the order of the sections.
- **The quizzes:** *Open or closed* plays one of five eight-bar sections for each answer, in C, G, F, D or A. *Which form* plays one
  chart for each form, in C. So once students know the charts, they can recognize them rather than the form. Use it for listening
  practice, not as a test.
- **Section names:** the strip at the bottom shows the section while the band plays (in a quiz, only after the answer).
- **Not here:** intros, pre-choruses, post-choruses and codas, and the book's song timelines (the songs are under copyright). The book's
  chapter has no video clips.
- **Not checked by ear:** the demos were checked by a test that plays each one and checks the notes are written out. Whether they sound
  convincing has not been checked by listening.
- The text on this page is written for the site, not copied from the book (the book is under the GNU Free Documentation License).
:::
